drills.q: Explain why fixed-epsilon greedy has linear regret while UCB1 has logarithmic regret.
drills.a: Fixed epsilon spends a constant fraction of all steps on uniform random actions forever, regardless of accumulated evidence, so regret accrues at a constant rate -> O(epsilon*T). UCB1's bonus term shrinks as N(a) grows, so exploration of confidently-bad arms fades over time while still occasionally revisiting any arm (bonus grows slowly with t) -> O(log T).

drills.q: A production ad-serving Thompson sampling bandit suddenly shows dropping revenue with no code change. Diagnose and propose a fix.
drills.a: Likely a non-stationary shift in the reward distribution (seasonality, new user cohort). Thompson sampling assumes stationarity; large accumulated alpha/beta counts make the posterior slow to move even against new contradicting evidence. Fix: discount/window the posterior updates (decay alpha,beta before each update) or add change-point detection triggering a reset.

drills.q: Someone says 'just increase epsilon, we're not exploring enough.' When is this the wrong fix, and what should you check instead?
drills.a: Wrong if the problem is unfocused exploration (uniform, ignoring what's already known) rather than insufficient volume -- raising epsilon wastes more budget re-testing known-bad arms. Check whether it's reward sparsity (needs intrinsic motivation, not more randomness) or whether exploration should be uncertainty-weighted (switch to UCB/Thompson instead of a bigger epsilon).

drills.q: Design an exploration strategy for a sparse-reward robotics task where reward only appears at final task success, hundreds of steps away.
drills.a: Value-uncertainty methods (epsilon-greedy/UCB/Thompson) need some nonzero reward to be uncertain about, which sparse reward may never provide via random exploration. Add intrinsic motivation (RND preferred over forward-model curiosity, since real robot sensors are noisy and would trigger the noisy-TV problem) with total reward r_ext + beta*r_int, tuning or annealing beta so novelty doesn't override the actual task objective.

drills.q: Why is exploration in RLHF/LLM RL considered fundamentally different from classic bandit exploration despite the same action-reward-update framing?
drills.a: The action space (all possible token sequences) is astronomically large, nowhere close to the small enumerable arm sets UCB/Thompson are built for -- no tractable confidence bound or posterior per possible response exists. Practice substitutes cruder mechanisms (sampling temperature, multi-rollout diversity, entropy bonuses) with none of the regret guarantees classic bandit methods provide.

drills.q: An agent's intrinsic reward stays high and behavior looks obsessive around one part of the environment, while task success stays at zero. Diagnose.
drills.a: Likely the noisy-TV problem: a forward-dynamics curiosity signal is stuck on a stochastic, unpredictable environment element (e.g. sensor noise) that can never be predicted, so prediction error (and thus intrinsic reward) never decreases there. Fix by switching to RND, whose target is a fixed deterministic random network rather than a stochastic environment outcome.
